title: Online Judge (LeetCode)
summary: Design a coding platform that safely runs submitted code against tests and ranks contest participants.
statement: Design an online judge. Users submit code in several languages; the system compiles and runs it in isolation against hidden test cases with time and memory limits, returns a verdict, and powers live contests with leaderboards. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.

requirementQuestions.question: How many submissions per second normally and during a contest?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: How quickly should a verdict return?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Defines which paths need caching, precomputation, or regional placement.

requirementQuestions.question: How is untrusted code isolated from the platform and from other submissions?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Introduces authentication, authorisation, and privacy constraints that affect the design.

requirementQuestions.question: How are verdicts made reproducible and fair across machines?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Selects between strong and eventual models and shapes conflict handling.

requirementQuestions.question: Which languages and special judges are supported?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

requirementQuestions.question: What happens to submissions during a contest peak?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: How many sandbox runs per second at peak?
How much CPU capacity must be reserved for contests?
How large is the test data to distribute?

keyDecisions.question: How are submissions processed?
considerations: Persist the submission, enqueue it, and let workers pull jobs.

keyDecisions.question: How is untrusted code isolated?
considerations: Containers or microVMs with seccomp, cgroups, no network, and read-only filesystems.

keyDecisions.question: How is test data managed?
considerations: Test cases in object storage cached on workers.

keyDecisions.question: How is live ranking served?
considerations: Verdict events update a sorted structure.
Freeze scoreboard near the end if needed.

tradeoffs.tension: MicroVMs are safer but slower than containers.
Fairness versus responsiveness for practice users.

commonMistakes: Running user code on application servers.
Allowing network access from the sandbox.
One shared queue so practice traffic starves contests.
Ignoring fork bombs and resource exhaustion.
followUps: How do you support interactive problems?
How do you add a new language?
How do you handle a judge worker crash mid-run?
